newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French deficit running at 3.5-3.7 pct -audit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French deficit running at 3.5-3.7 pct -audit.

text.p: An audit of French public finances found that this year's public deficit is running at between 3.5 and 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, auditor Jacques Bonnet said on Monday, citing a figure well above the criterion for European monetary union.
He was speaking to reporters after presenting a report by two experts from the state Court of Auditors to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.

Asked what figure they had given for the total deficit on the state budget and welfare accounts in 1997, the reference year for meeting the Maastricht treaty goal of three percent to qualify for a single European currency, he said: "3.5-3.7, we give a range."
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn was due to announce the full findings of the audit and a package of tax and savings measures at a news conference at 10.30 a.m. (0830 GMT).

Government sources said the main measure would be an increase in corporate tax on big business aimed at bringing this year's deficit down to within reach of the three percent target, although Strauss-Kahn has said France's will not make a strict 3.0 percent.
Jospin put final touches to the measures at the weekend.
Government sources have said corporate tax would be increased to an effective rate of about 40 percent, from 36.6 percent at present, and the increase may be extended in 1998.
Dubbed a "euro surcharge" by French newspapers, the tax rise is expected to raise 12 billion francs ($2 billion) this year.

Companies could also be hit by a rise in the current 19 percent tax on capital gains on sales of assets. But small and medium firms, seen as key to job creation in the battle to cut 12.5 percent unemployment, would be spared.
The government is also mulling a rise in employers' pension contributions, and could tap state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations for a contribution to fill budget gaps.

The tax increases are meant to ensure France qualifies for monetary union while fulfilling a Socialist Party campaign pledge ahead of the June 1 parliamentary election not to impose new austerity on French people.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said Strauss-Kahn had telephoned him to assure him France would do everything necessary to meet targets for European monetary union.
He also defended the French government's plans, saying any tax increases were not creative accounting, but real measures. However, they should be followed by structural reform.

Share prices fell further in early trading on the Paris Bourse on Monday, the third successive day of losses largely due to concern about the expected measures. The CAC-40 index fell 1.2 percent in the first 15 minutes of trading.

But bonds were little changed, while the franc was marginally weaker at 3.3807/12 per mark compared to 3.3783 on Friday. Analysts have said most of the bad news on the French audit is already built into prices.
They have said markets will look as much at plans for next year, amid hopes Strauss-Kahn will reaffirm a commitment to reduce the deficit to three percent of GDP in 1998.
